analysis.one_liner: Funds long-term health monitoring for 9/11 responders and residents with a 1% surtax on income over $500,000.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2004, never received a hearing or vote in either committee it was sent to, and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a federal trust fund to pay for medical screening, clinical exams, and up to 20 years of health monitoring for people exposed to toxic dust after the September 11 attacks — firefighters, police, cleanup workers, and people who lived or worked near Ground Zero. The money would come from a new 1% tax on adjusted gross income above $1 million for married couples filing jointly and above $500,000 for everyone else. It would also fund federal research into 9/11-related illnesses and let the Health Secretary set up a similar program for Pentagon attack responders.
analysis.who_benefits: Up to 40,000 or more people exposed to World Trade Center dust: emergency and rescue personnel, cleanup and recovery workers, transit workers, and residents, students, and workers in the declared disaster area. The bill designated part of the funding for active and retired New York City firefighters and named the FDNY program and an existing consortium of medical providers as award recipients. It also would have funded NIH research into 9/11-related conditions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: 9/11 responders and residents near Ground Zero

how_it_helps.text: Creates a September 11 Emergency Personnel Trust Fund to pay for baseline and follow-up screenings, clinical exams, and long-term health monitoring for covered individuals, capped at 20 years per person with a minimum enrollment of 40,000 people.

Covers a broad group: emergency service and rescue personnel, cleanup and infrastructure restoration workers, police, firefighters, EMTs, transit workers, federal and state employees, and people who lived, worked, or attended school or child care in the declared disaster area.

Directs NIH to conduct or support diagnostic and treatment research for 9/11-related health conditions, in consultation with the medical consortium, the FDNY, and the firefighters' union, with annual reports to Congress.

Allows the Health Secretary to extend treatment services to enrolled covered individuals who have no other means of obtaining treatment, and to set up a similar program for Pentagon attack responders.

The bill's findings cite research linking World Trade Center dust to persistent cough, asthma, reduced infant birth weight, and elevated future risks including mesothelioma from asbestos exposure found in the rubble.

analysis.who_pays: A new 1% tax on adjusted gross income above $1 million for joint filers and above $500,000 for other filers, effective for tax years after 2004, would fall entirely on high-income households.

drawbacks.text: The bill limits monitoring to 20 years per person and to no fewer than 40,000 enrollees, which the Secretary could exceed only if determined appropriate — a cap that later 9/11 health programs outgrew as new conditions like cancers emerged over time.

The funding is a dedicated surtax on high incomes rather than general revenue, so the program's existence is tied to that tax continuing; the bill appropriates only the amounts raised by the 1% surtax.

Award recipients are effectively narrowed to the existing FDNY program and the specific consortium that provided these services in fiscal year 2003, reducing competition and flexibility in how the care is delivered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a documented, ongoing health crisis among 9/11 responders and area residents, and the cost was a narrow 1% surtax on incomes above $500,000 — a small share of the population. The main design weaknesses were the 20-year and 40,000-person limits and the near-exclusive reliance on two existing provider programs, but the core trade-off was modest cost to wealthy households for sustained medical monitoring of people exposed to known toxins.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to two committees and a health subcommittee on the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York introduced the bill on July 22, 2004.
The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and its health provisions were referred to the Subcommittee on Health.
No further action was taken: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion appears in the record.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and all legislation not passed expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households that would have paid the new 1% surtax are better off because the bill never advanced; 9/11 responders and residents got no new federal health monitoring program from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income households that would have paid the surtax

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so the record shows no measurable partisan support either way.

industries.note: The bill's funding mechanism is a 1% surtax on adjusted gross income above $500,000 ($1 million for joint filers), so this group would have borne the entire cost. The surtax applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2004.

industries.industry: 9/11 medical monitoring programs (FDNY program and the academic medical consortium)
industries.note: The bill would route grants from the trust fund to the New York City Fire Department program and the consortium of medical entities that had provided these health services in fiscal 2003, giving them a dedicated federal revenue stream.

industries.industry: Medical research institutions (NIH and its grantees)
industries.note: The bill directs NIH funding toward diagnostic and treatment research on 9/11-related health conditions, paid from the same trust fund.
